reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes BitClub Network participation by directing viewers to register, pay a membership fee and a $500 mining-pool package in Bitcoin, and use shown wallet addresses and QR-code payment pages. It presents mining-pool balances, daily withdrawal or reinvestment settings, and team commissions as benefits of participating, making the tutorial a solicitation for paid cryptocurrency-earning participation. The speaker's limited expertise and the lack of proof about mining performance, payout authenticity, or user losses do not change the observed offer and earnings claims.

You can change this to 50 percent if you want and start to withdraw Bitcoin everyday if you want. But I think it's best to leave it at 100% for a few months just to build it up a little bit quicker.

opening.argument: Judge this as a candid account of one person's experience, not a promise of returns. The speaker says, "I don't claim to be an expert in this business yet" and describes the new participant as someone who "just wants to test it" [1][2]. His suggestion to reinvest is framed as a preference: "I think it's best to leave it at 100% for a few months" [3]. Those qualifications matter. He shows what he is doing and what he currently thinks, without claiming that the same result is assured for a viewer.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited fees and withdrawal setting establish what this participant chose to buy and how he configured the account; they do not establish a guaranteed yield or that every viewer will receive one. The speaker expressly calls the new participant's entry a test [1]. A payment walkthrough can document a transaction without proving that the speaker has verified future mining performance.

citations.quote: he just wants to test it

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A qualification about expertise does not undo the invitation to participate. The description tells viewers to "Register at Bitclub Network and start earning bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies on daily basis" [1]. The speaker then explains a $99 membership fee and $500 mining-pool investment [2], followed by a setting he says can be used to withdraw Bitcoin every day [3]. Calling one person's purchase a test does not change the offer being promoted.

opening.argument: The video's organizing purpose is operational: its title calls it a "tutorial purchase" [1], and the speaker introduces it as a video on "setting up an account and buying a mining pool package" [2]. He works in another person's account because that person has computer difficulties and asked him to handle the setup [3]. The Coinbase explanation, barcode payment and order-history check follow that task. A careful reading distinguishes showing how a particular purchase was completed from certifying the underlying mining business or promising viewers a payout.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening accurately identifies payment steps, but those are precisely the steps a purchase tutorial would cover. The speaker says the account belongs to someone else [1], and the order-history view records the payment as pending confirmation [2]. Neither detail proves mining output or future withdrawals; the demonstrated outcome is an account transaction, not a verified return.

citations.quote: obviously this is not my account this is one of my guys accounts

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A tutorial can still solicit participation. The accompanying description explicitly asks viewers to register and start earning daily [1]. The walkthrough then shows how to pay for the mining-pool package [2], and the speaker explains a setting for daily Bitcoin withdrawals [3]. Those details make the procedure a route into the paid earning offer, not merely an account-management lesson.

You can change this to 50 percent if you want and start to withdraw Bitcoin everyday if you want.

opening.argument: The visible transaction has defined prices rather than a hidden charge: the speaker separates a one-time $99 membership fee from the $500 mining-pool purchase [1]. The membership page lists included features [2], and the speaker checks order history after paying [3]. That is evidence of a paid membership and purchase flow. It is not, by itself, evidence that the displayed mining figures are false, that a payout was refused, or that a viewer lost funds. Even the speaker's commission account is a reported personal result, not a demonstrated guarantee to a purchaser.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference opening treats the price and daily settings as decisive. They show an offered service and account controls, but not whether the service actually mined Bitcoin or whether the speaker's account figures were paid out. The order-history step shows a transaction being tracked [1]; it does not settle those separate questions. Nor does describing his own team commissions establish that this particular purchaser must recruit to use the package.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The concern is the offer the video promotes, not a proven loss or a mandatory recruitment rule. The description directs viewers to register for daily cryptocurrency earnings [1]. The speaker calls the $500 payment a mining-pool investment [2] and links bringing in people to a daily commission level for his team [3]. An itemized checkout and order history do not remove those paid-return and recruitment claims.
